content.headline: US midterms put control of Congress and Trump’s final two years at stake
content.shortHeadline: US midterms test Trump and could reshape Congress
content.standfirst: Voters are choosing all 435 House members and 35 senators in a contest shaped by the cost of living, the Iran war and Trump’s record. Polls suggest Democrats could gain, but the outcome—and the timing of results—remain uncertain.

image.caption: Voters cast ballots in Detroit during early voting for the US midterms.

sources.originalTitle: Americans head to polls in midterm elections seen as referendum on Trump
Americans head to the polls for elections that could define Trump's closing chapter
12 milliarder dollar på spil: Midtvejsvalget står til at blive det dyreste nogensinde

segments.body: Americans are voting in midterm elections that will determine control of the House and Senate for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency. Democrats are aiming to limit his legislative agenda and investigate his administration; polling points to a possible House gain, while the Senate is a harder contest.

segments.title: A campaign shaped by costs
segments.body: The Iran war and rising prices have featured heavily in the campaign, alongside concerns about government conduct. The result is not a straightforward verdict on Trump: reporting from voters and analysts describes frustration with his policies, but also doubts that discontent will automatically translate into votes for Democrats. The outcome may take time to establish in close races.

segments.title: Record spending
segments.body: A forecast cited by DR puts total midterm spending at about $11.9bn, which would make this the most expensive midterm cycle on record. Political groups have already spent billions on advertising and voter outreach.

perspectives.body: DR’s account highlights Elon Musk as a leading donor: it reports that he has given at least $445.77m to Republican-aligned groups since last year, including $216m to his own America PAC.

content.headline: Trump says US will end annual aid to Israel, but details remain unclear
content.shortHeadline: Trump says US aid to Israel will end this year
content.standfirst: The president says a deal with Benjamin Netanyahu will stop $4bn in yearly funding by the end of 2026. The White House has not clarified what he means; the current US-Israel military-aid agreement runs through 2028.

image.caption: US aid to Israel has become a politically contentious issue.

sources.originalTitle: Trump says US will stop providing aid to Israel after year-end

segments.body: Donald Trump has said the US will stop providing funding to Israel at the end of this year, claiming he reached an agreement with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu months ago. The White House has been asked to clarify his remarks, and Netanyahu’s office has not commented.

segments.title: What the existing deal says
segments.body: The scale and timing of any change remain uncertain. A memorandum of understanding provides Israel with $3.8bn a year in military assistance and expires at the end of 2028. Trump referred to $4bn and said the US might still help Israel if needed, without explaining what future arrangement he had in mind.

content.headline: Binance says fake job interviews helped hackers steal $6.3bn in crypto
content.shortHeadline: Binance says hackers used fake interviews in $6.3bn theft
content.standfirst: The crypto exchange says an engineer was tricked into downloading malware during a bogus job interview, giving attackers access to internal systems. US agencies blame North Korea; Pyongyang denies involvement.

sources.originalTitle: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack

segments.body: Binance says attackers stole a record $6.3bn in cryptocurrency from its own wallets after targeting engineers with fake job interviews. The company says one engineer was asked to download a malicious file disguised as an interview assignment, allowing hackers to compromise computers and access other internal systems.

segments.title: Attribution remains contested
segments.body: The attack forced Binance to suspend customer withdrawals until service was restored on Sunday. The company says it has replenished 98% of affected token assets and set aside more than enough funds to cover the loss. The FBI and other US agencies attribute the hack to North Korea; Pyongyang denies responsibility.

content.headline: US urges Venezuela to free remaining political prisoners as reforms stall
content.shortHeadline: US presses Venezuela to free 322 political detainees
content.standfirst: Marco Rubio raised the release of prisoners and electoral reform in talks with Venezuela’s foreign minister. Rights group Foro Penal says 322 people remain detained; the interim president has not set a date for elections.

image.caption: Venezuelan Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met on Monday.

sources.originalTitle: US urges Venezuela to release remaining political prisoners

segments.body: The US has urged Venezuela’s interim government to release people still held as political prisoners. Secretary of State Marco Rubio raised the issue and electoral reform in a meeting with Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco, according to the US State Department. Foro Penal says 322 people remain in detention, after more than 1,000 were freed since Nicolás Maduro was seized by US forces in January.

segments.title: No election date set
segments.body: The pace and timetable of political change remain disputed. The Trump administration has called for quick reform of Venezuela’s election system, while interim president Delcy Rodríguez has said there will be elections but given no date. Opposition leader María Corina Machado has called for a vote next year.

content.headline: US moves to remove South Africa and Rwanda from preferential trade programme
content.shortHeadline: Trump moves to remove South Africa and Rwanda from US trade deal
content.standfirst: The administration says both countries no longer meet eligibility rules for duty-free exports under Agoa. South Africa calls the decision unfortunate; the effect is likely to differ sharply between the two economies.

image.caption: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa met Donald Trump at the White House last year.

sources.originalTitle: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal

segments.body: Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from the African Growth and Opportunity Act, which allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US without tariffs. The administration cited trade barriers and concerns about national security and foreign policy.

segments.title: Different exposure to the change
segments.body: South Africa’s trade minister called the move “unfortunate” and said Washington had raised new issues. Government figures cited in the report say around 10% of South African exports to the US benefited from Agoa in 2025. Rwanda’s exports are less exposed: an economist quoted by the BBC estimates the US accounted for about 2% of its merchandise exports, and only around 4% of its US-bound exports used Agoa preferences.

content.headline: China steps up Gulf diplomacy as US-Iran talks continue
content.shortHeadline: China courts Gulf leaders as Iran talks continue
content.standfirst: Xi Jinping has met Oman’s sultan, while China’s foreign minister held talks with Saudi and Iranian officials. Beijing is presenting itself as a potential regional mediator, though its role in the conflict has so far been limited.

image.caption: China’s President Xi Jinping welcomes Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq in Beijing.

sources.originalTitle: Trump’s troubles with Iran could open the door to China

segments.body: China has intensified diplomatic contacts in the Gulf ahead of an expected meeting between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump later this month. Xi met Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq in Beijing, while Foreign Minister Wang Yi met Saudi and Iranian officials.

segments.title: Influence and limits
segments.body: Beijing says it wants to help bring lasting peace, and an analyst quoted by the Guardian says its investment and trade give it influence in the region. But China has done little to broker an end to the war so far. Disruption to the Strait of Hormuz also poses risks to its economy, while renewed US military action could further raise tensions.

content.headline: UK and EU settle food deal to remove most post-Brexit checks
content.shortHeadline: UK-EU deal would remove most food checks—but not until 2028
content.standfirst: The agreement would cut certificates and inspections for many food, animal and plant products moving between Britain and the EU. It is expected to take effect in early 2028, after legislation and a transition period.

image.caption: Lorries queue on the road to Dover, where the deal is intended to reduce paperwork and checks on exports.

sources.originalTitle: UK and EU agree deal to remove Brexit checks on food and animal products
The UK-EU food produce deal: what was agreed and will it affect shoppers?

segments.body: The UK and EU have settled the text of a deal intended to remove most certificates and checks on food, animals, plants and related products traded between them. The agreement would ease the movement of goods including meat, cheese, fish, plants and leather products, but is not yet in force.

segments.title: Benefits—and a long wait
segments.body: The deal is expected to be implemented in early 2028, after Britain aligns relevant legislation with EU rules and a transition period for some products. It could make exports easier and restore some options for British retailers and consumers. Most checks on agricultural goods moving from Great Britain to Northern Ireland would also end, though the Democratic Unionist party says the agreement does not go far enough.

content.headline: PIP claims become harder to win as award rates fall, analysis finds
content.shortHeadline: Fewer new PIP claims are being awarded, analysis finds
content.standfirst: The share of new applicants awarded Personal Independence Payment after assessment fell from 54% in April 2024 to 42%, according to figures analysed by the i Paper. Advisers say assessments have become harsher; ministers are reviewing the system.

image.caption: Disabled activists protest against proposed changes to PIP.

sources.originalTitle: The hidden crackdown on PIP as benefit assessments get tougher

segments.body: The proportion of new Personal Independence Payment claims resulting in an award after assessment has fallen to 42%, from 54% in April 2024, analysis of Department for Work and Pensions figures by the i Paper shows. About 4.1 million people currently receive PIP, which supports daily living and mobility needs.

segments.title: Claims of tougher decisions
segments.body: Benefits advisers and a former assessor say decisions are increasingly going against applicants, including people with fluctuating conditions and some who are in work. The government’s Office for Budget Responsibility has also said a lower proportion of claims are being awarded after assessment. The government says a review is under way and that PIP is no longer fit for purpose; the causes of the falling award rate are not independently established in this report.

content.headline: Jury retires to consider verdicts in Russell Brand rape trial
content.shortHeadline: Jury begins deliberations in Russell Brand trial
content.standfirst: The jury at Southwark Crown Court is considering seven charges against the comedian, who denies them all. The allegations relate to six women and span 1999 to 2009.

image.caption: Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court in London.

sources.originalTitle: Jury in Russell Brand rape trial begins considering verdicts
Jury in Russell Brand rape and sexual assault trial retires to consider verdicts

segments.body: A jury has begun considering its verdicts in Russell Brand’s trial at Southwark Crown Court. Brand has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault, relating to allegations by six women between 1999 and 2009.

segments.title: Prosecution and defence arguments
segments.body: The prosecution told jurors that the women described a similar pattern of behaviour and said their accounts were credible. Brand’s barrister argued that a 2023 media investigation had “poisoned the wells” of justice and questioned the delay in reporting. The judge told the jury he could accept only a unanimous verdict.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s account sets out the opposing closing arguments in more detail: the prosecution said the six women had nothing to gain by coming forward, while the defence pointed to delays and the impact of earlier media coverage.

content.headline: UK proposes default lifetime pension income for private-sector savers
content.shortHeadline: New pension plan would offer private workers income for life
content.standfirst: Ministers propose guided retirement options for 17 million workers, including a default designed to provide income throughout retirement. Savers would still be able to choose how to use their pension pots.

image.caption: The government says its pension proposals are intended to offer more workers an income throughout retirement.

sources.originalTitle: Guaranteed pension income ‘resurrected’ for 17m private sector workers

segments.body: The government plans to offer private-sector pension savers a default retirement option designed to provide an income for life, with payments in many cases linked to inflation. The proposal would affect 17 million workers, many of whom now retire with a savings pot to manage rather than a guaranteed pension.

segments.title: Choice remains
segments.body: The plan is intended to make retirement decisions simpler after nearly half of pension pots accessed for the first time in 2025-26 were emptied, according to the government. Savers would still be able to withdraw money or invest elsewhere. Pension experts quoted in the report support a simpler option but stress that people should retain freedom to choose.

content.headline: UK meat suppliers report freezer cyber incidents after attacks in Europe
content.shortHeadline: UK meat suppliers report freezer cyber incidents
content.standfirst: Some British suppliers say refrigeration units were affected, but the industry body reports no meat was lost and says affected units were empty. The National Cyber Security Centre says the national impact is minimal and has not identified who was responsible.

image.caption: A worker clears a refrigerated display unit after a hacking incident at a supermarket in Sweden.

sources.originalTitle: Freezers of UK meat suppliers heat up after cyber-attacks in Europe

segments.body: UK meat suppliers have reported cyber incidents after hackers accessed supermarket refrigeration systems in several European countries. The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers says some of its members were affected, but no meat was lost and the units involved were empty at the time.

segments.title: Responsibility unknown
segments.body: The National Cyber Security Centre says the UK impact is minimal and that it is working with affected organisations. Researchers found activity against decoy fridge controls resembling infrastructure previously associated with Russian-linked operations, but said they could not identify a group responsible. The NCSC said the incidents used long-known vulnerabilities and were not AI-enabled.

content.headline: Reform UK council leader charged with rape and other offences
content.shortHeadline: Reform UK council leader charged with 12 counts of rape
content.standfirst: George Madgwick faces charges relating to four complainants who were teenagers at the time, according to the Crown Prosecution Service. He is due in court on 25 November and has been suspended by Reform UK.

image.caption: George Madgwick, Reform UK’s group leader on Hampshire County Council.

sources.originalTitle: Reform UK councillor charged with 12 counts of rape and multiple other offences

segments.body: George Madgwick, Reform UK’s group leader on Hampshire County Council, has been charged with 12 counts of rape and multiple other offences. The Crown Prosecution Service says the charges relate to four complainants, aged 16 and 17 at the time, and alleged offences between 2008 and 2021. Madgwick is due to appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on 25 November.

segments.title: Party response
segments.body: Reform UK says Madgwick has been suspended with immediate effect. The CPS says proceedings are active and reminds the public that the defendant has the right to a fair trial. No plea is reported in the gathered account.

content.headline: Cern particle result raises questions over UK role in future research
content.shortHeadline: New particle result points to tiny scale; UK funding remains in doubt
content.standfirst: Researchers at the Large Hadron Collider have detected beauty-quark interactions at the smallest scale yet explored, a result that may help test ideas about dark matter. UK scientists warn funding decisions could limit their future role.

sources.originalTitle: Scientists detect signals at the smallest scale ever explored

segments.body: Scientists working with the LHCb experiment at Cern say they have detected beauty quarks interacting at distances about 100 billion times smaller than an atom. The finding does not detect dark matter, but researchers say further measurements could help test theories about how particles behave at these scales.

segments.title: UK funding at issue
segments.body: The result comes as UK researchers question whether funding decisions will affect their involvement in a planned detector upgrade. The collaboration’s leader says the UK risks missing major discoveries and training opportunities. UK Research and Innovation says it remains a fully engaged Cern member and its second-largest funder, contributing about £175m a year.

content.headline: Greenland pauses approval of US defence deal amid political dispute
content.shortHeadline: Greenland pauses US defence deal vote after confidentiality row
content.standfirst: Greenland’s parliament paused its approval process after the government accused opposition party Naleraq of disclosing confidential committee information. Naleraq denies that the material came from a closed meeting and says it will back the deal if the foreign minister resigns.

image.caption: Greenland’s parliament resumes debate on the defence agreement with the US.

sources.originalTitle: Grønlands regering anklager parti for brud på tavshedspligt: Godkendelse af USA-aftale sat på pause i Grønland

segments.body: Greenland’s parliament has paused its process to approve a defence agreement signed by Greenland, the US and Denmark in September. The pause followed an accusation by Foreign Affairs Minister Múte B. Egede that opposition party Naleraq disclosed information shared in a closed parliamentary committee meeting. The parliamentary presidium has reported the party to police.

segments.title: Competing accounts
segments.body: Naleraq leader Pele Broberg says there is no evidence the party’s statement came from a confidential meeting, and says it was based on notes from an information meeting. The party has filed a no-confidence motion against Egede and says it will not support the agreement unless he takes responsibility and resigns.

content.headline: Flights across Europe targeted by threats, including SAS service from Copenhagen
content.shortHeadline: SAS flight from Copenhagen among European flights threatened
content.standfirst: Several flights, including a Copenhagen-Warsaw SAS service, landed safely after threats. Searches reported no explosives, but it remains unclear who made the threats or whether the incidents are connected.

image.caption: A passenger aboard the SAS flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw after it landed following a threat.

sources.originalTitle: Flere trusler mod europæiske fly i dag: Danskere var på SAS-fly til Polen
Four planes flying across Europe targeted by bomb threats
Flights from Manchester, Luton and Heathrow targeted by suspected bomb threats

segments.body: Multiple flights across Europe were targeted by threats, including SAS flight SK751 from Copenhagen to Warsaw. The plane landed normally and passengers left it at Warsaw’s Chopin airport. Other affected flights included services from London and Manchester; the threats’ source and any connection between incidents are unknown.

The flights landed safely, and searches reported by the Guardian and the i Paper found no explosives. Passenger Peter Leschly told DR that the SAS passengers were taken by bus to a waiting area while police dogs checked luggage; he described the process as calm.

perspectives.body: DR’s passenger account adds a first-hand description of the response on the Copenhagen-Warsaw flight: Leschly said passengers waited at the airport after leaving the aircraft and that the episode proceeded peacefully.

content.headline: National Museum of Denmark plans further job cuts as visitor numbers fall
content.shortHeadline: National Museum plans job cuts after visitor numbers fall
content.standfirst: The museum expects lower income and higher IT costs, including spending on cyber security after an attack this summer. It plans changes intended to free up DKK 11m–13m.

image.caption: The National Museum of Denmark is planning further job cuts as visitor numbers decline.

sources.originalTitle: Nationalmuseet nedlægger stillinger

segments.body: The National Museum of Denmark says falling visitor numbers across its 15 sites and rising IT costs will require further cuts to its budget. It plans to reduce positions and reorganise parts of the institution to free up DKK 11m–13m.

The museum says higher cyber-security costs follow an attack that hit it hard this summer. Director Rane Willerslev also points to visitors having less money to spend after higher travel and accommodation costs. The museum receives half its funding from state grants and raises the other half itself.

content.headline: Queen Margrethe presents journalism award to Greenlandic editor
content.shortHeadline: Greenlandic editor receives Ebbe Munck journalism award
content.standfirst: Masaana Egede, editor-in-chief of Sermitsiaq, received the Ebbe Munck Prize 2026 at Fredensborg Palace. The award recognises the newspaper’s work informing Greenlanders in two languages during heightened geopolitical attention.

image.caption: Masaana Egede receives the Ebbe Munck Prize 2026 from Queen Margrethe.

sources.originalTitle: Dronning Margrethe overækker pris til grønlandsk chefredaktør

segments.body: Queen Margrethe presented the Ebbe Munck Prize 2026 to Masaana Egede, editor-in-chief of Greenlandic newspaper Sermitsiaq, at Fredensborg Palace. DR says the award recognises her journalism and the outlet’s work keeping Greenland’s population informed in two languages during heightened attention to US ambitions concerning Greenland.

content.headline: Can a global music project help bring climate grief to COP31?
content.shortHeadline: The artists bringing climate grief to COP31
content.standfirst: Flow brings women artists from across the world together for an album centred on water, with Charlotte Church, Maxine Peake and others taking its music to the climate summit in Turkey. Its creators hope feeling can help move the debate beyond awareness.

image.caption: Charlotte Church, whose Flow song “My Mother, the Ocean” moves from a water-inspired piece to an expression of grief and anger.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Music is the most powerful way of connecting to what’s happening’: can this album change your mind about the climate crisis?

segments.body: Flow began with musicians meeting online after a UN official was moved by women singing about water at last year’s climate summit in Brazil. The project has grown into an album, co-produced by Jennifer Decilveo, featuring artists including Charlotte Church, Maxine Peake and Nadine Shah. This month, the collective is due to perform at COP31 in Turkey.

segments.title: From awareness to action
segments.body: The album’s songs draw on artists’ different relationships to water. Shingai sings in Shona, while Márcia Mura, an Indigenous teacher from the Brazilian Amazon, describes rivers damaged by floods, drought, dams and pollution. She stresses that Indigenous women must speak for themselves and says protecting the river is bound up with protecting lives.

Church’s contribution, “My Mother, the Ocean”, moves from a sound-healing piece into distorted electropop expressing grief and anger. The project will also soundtrack a documentary about women on the frontlines of the climate crisis. Flow’s organisers argue that music can connect people emotionally to what data alone cannot; whether it can help bring about political change remains an open question.

content.headline: Bernie Taupin steps out alone with a late-life musical manifesto
content.shortHeadline: Bernie Taupin’s solo album, on his own terms
content.standfirst: The lyricist behind much of Elton John’s catalogue has released a new solo record on which he wrote the music as well as the words. He talks about finding room to be himself, from the album’s rants to his love of anonymity and rodeo.

image.caption: Bernie Taupin, whose new solo album includes music and lyrics written by him.

sources.originalTitle: ‘At my age, I can rant!’ Bernie Taupin on Elton John, hellraising vampires and competing in full-blown rodeos

segments.body: Bernie Taupin has released The Sea Has No Mercy, a solo album recorded in Nashville with producer Frank Liddell. Unlike his earlier solo efforts, Taupin wrote both lyrics and music this time. He describes it as “100% selfish” and a late-life manifesto: a reflective record that can turn wistful, grouchy or exuberant.

segments.title: The man behind the words
segments.body: Taupin is best known as Elton John’s songwriting partner, but says he values the relative anonymity that comes with being recognised only after someone sees his name on a credit card. He recalls how songs can take on new meanings when John sings them: “I’m Still Standing”, for instance, began as a message to an ex-girlfriend, though listeners heard John’s own story of resilience.

The interview also traces the life outside the partnership: Taupin’s 1970s Hollywood Vampires drinking circle, his move to the US and his enthusiasm for rodeo. He plans to perform one show for the album at Nashville’s Grand Ole Opry, alongside his daughter Georgey, and says a career-spanning documentary is due later this year.

content.headline: Skepta’s long-awaited album turns grime’s elder statesman into a conscience
content.shortHeadline: Skepta returns with a more conscious sound
content.standfirst: On The Fork and Knife, the grime star reflects on past mistakes and takes aim at anti-immigrant rhetoric, while keeping the genre’s energy and bringing younger MCs into the frame. He tells the Guardian how fatherhood and British rap history shaped the record.

image.caption: Skepta, whose new album combines grime with reflections on immigration, identity and responsibility.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Ignorance towards immigration is horrible. It’s not British’: Skepta on his long-awaited return – and his anger at the racist right

segments.body: Skepta says he has tried to make The Fork and Knife, his first full solo album since 2019, both socially conscious and still enjoyable to hear. He describes growing more aware of what his words carry as a father, and says he wants to speak about politics without sounding preachy. The album was first announced in January 2024, after a long period of work.

segments.title: A British story
segments.body: The single “Innocent Smile”, featuring Suggs and breakbeats from Chase and Status, argues for a multicultural Britain and criticises politicians who scapegoat immigrants. Skepta connects that outlook to his own family and upbringing: his Nigerian parents met in England, and he recalls a home where his father’s ska records brought together different communities.

The 15 tracks range from a zouk-flavoured R&B collaboration with Aya Nakamura to “Belly”, an eight-minute grime track with younger MCs. Skepta also revisits earlier missteps, including the album artwork that inadvertently evoked the Holocaust and his past Puma deal, which he later regretted. He says he remains a student, still learning how to use his voice responsibly.

content.headline: Richard Thompson revisits Fairport Convention’s grief and his new album
content.shortHeadline: Richard Thompson on grief, memory and new songs
content.standfirst: The folk guitarist discusses Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, the 20th solo album of a six-decade career, and the 1969 crash that killed Fairport Convention drummer Martin Lamble and Thompson’s girlfriend Jeannie Franklyn. He says the band did not know how to deal with the loss.

image.caption: Richard Thompson, whose new album draws on characters and memories from his life.

sources.originalTitle: Fairport Convention’s Richard Thompson on the crash that killed his bandmate

segments.body: Richard Thompson has released Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, his 20th solo album. The interview ranges from the record’s characters and his long creative career to the early days of Fairport Convention, which he formed in 1967. Thompson says he still wants English folk to sound rooted in its own culture, even though he has lived in the United States for much of the past 35 years.

segments.title: A loss they could not process
segments.body: In May 1969, a road accident killed Fairport drummer Martin Lamble, 19, and Thompson’s girlfriend, Jeannie Franklyn. Thompson, who was in the van, recalls trying to reach Franklyn after the crash. “We did not deal with it,” he says. The band returned to work and made Liege and Lief, but he describes the next two years as a period of shock and grief.

Thompson reflects that the loss shaped the band’s departures and decisions, and says he, Ashley Hutchings and Simon Nicol still think about Lamble. Writing his memoir, he says, brought uncomfortable memories back into view rather than allowing them to be shut away again. The new album includes songs inspired by people and episodes from his past, as well as fictional characters.

content.headline: Kali Malone’s new organ album finds delicate detail in a sacred space
content.shortHeadline: Kali Malone finds new textures in the pipe organ
content.standfirst: On Burning Song, the composer makes short, melodic pieces with guitarist Stephen O’Malley and cellist Lucy Railton, recorded in Leipzig’s St Thomas Church. The result departs from the vast drones often associated with her work.

sources.originalTitle: Burning Song

segments.body: Burning Song is Kali Malone’s first solo album since 2024’s All Life Long. She returns to the pipe organ, accompanied by Stephen O’Malley on guitar and Lucy Railton on cello, but trades the expansive scale of much of her earlier work for pieces all under seven minutes. Their intertwined parts often make it hard to distinguish one instrument from another.

segments.title: A different kind of church music
segments.body: The trio recorded the album at St Thomas Church in Leipzig, where J.S. Bach is buried. Malone has described it as a church for music rather than a place centred on a saint. The organ was built in 2000, with tuning systems intended to reflect Bach’s era; the compositions themselves turn away from baroque forms and use the setting as a launch point for contemporary experiments.

The review hears a newly prominent melodic quality in the music. Tracks such as “Crawling Ashore” and “Map the Path” suggest movement and narrative, while the closing “My Eve My Dawn” circles around the idea that endings can give way to beginnings. Loss and uncertainty linger, but the record’s restraint and changing textures keep it from settling into a single mood.

content.headline: Lydia Loveless turns self-reproach into sharp, immediate songs on Accolades
content.shortHeadline: Lydia Loveless finds new direction on Accolades
content.standfirst: The Ohio songwriter’s new EP pairs caustic humour and vivid details with a growing curiosity about stability. Its title track appears twice, revealing how much Loveless can change a song through a shift in phrasing.

sources.originalTitle: Accolades EP

segments.body: Lydia Loveless wrote the songs on Accolades throughout 2025, posting one new song each month on Bandcamp. The EP’s title track and its reprise bookend the release, with a changed arrangement and delivery that alter the song’s tone. The review sees that variation as central to Loveless’s strength: they can reshape a song’s meaning through inflection and cadence.

segments.title: A little less chaos
segments.body: Loveless’s writing remains full of sharp turns, comic phrasing and unsparing details. “Oklahoma” describes a long-distance relationship against the backdrop of a crumbling apartment; “What We Learned?” turns a lover’s complaint about their father into a pointed joke. The reviewer finds the EP’s focus and immediacy partly shaped by the monthly-writing challenge.

The songs also hint at a change in direction. Where earlier records seemed to embrace chaos, this EP suggests Loveless is curious about a life with fewer bad habits and more stability. One torch song is less successful, the review argues, because its forceful delivery leaves less room for the nuance that makes the other tracks compelling.

content.headline: Two Shell’s Infinite Now prompts a fierce critique of AI and club-pop
content.shortHeadline: Two Shell’s AI debate can’t rescue Infinite Now
content.standfirst: Pitchfork argues that the duo’s new album is weighed down less by its use of AI than by music it finds dull and self-satisfied. The review says the group’s once-volatile sound has lost its spark, while noting that the tools behind the record remain unclear.

sources.originalTitle: Infinite Now

segments.body: Two Shell have defended using AI-powered tools, describing them as instruments, but their exact use on Infinite Now remains unconfirmed. The Pitchfork review says that distinction is not the album’s main problem: it hears a record whose mid-tempo tracks and synthetic-sounding vocals lack the volatility that made the duo’s earlier music compelling.

segments.title: A question of craft
segments.body: The reviewer contrasts Infinite Now with earlier work such as “Talk to Me”, which used filters and shifting volumes to create a sense of movement. Here, build-ups and drops are said to fall flat, and even the 55-track bonus collection is read as evidence of excess rather than inspiration. The review notes that fans have pointed to possible references to the music-generating app Suno, but says the evidence is not settled.

The criticism is not simply that AI is involved: the review’s central charge is that the album lacks effort, character and a coherent emotional thread. It leaves open whether Two Shell’s provocative stance is sincere or trolling, while arguing that either way the music itself fails to make the case for the project.

content.headline: Shovel Dance Collective reworks English folk songs as living social history
content.shortHeadline: Shovel Dance Collective makes folk music feel radical
content.standfirst: Everything in Readiness combines old songs about work, prisons and migration with drones, tape edits and field recordings. Pitchfork hears the London group connecting folk’s radical past to struggles that still resonate.

sources.originalTitle: Everything in Readiness

segments.body: London’s nine-piece Shovel Dance Collective takes its name from the idea of folk music as both a record of work and a respite from it. On Everything in Readiness, the group layers traditional songs and instruments with drone, tape manipulation and recordings made in different settings. The review argues that the result treats folk not as a preserved relic but as a tradition that can speak to the present.

segments.title: Songs that still speak
segments.body: The album’s arrangements connect different eras and sources. “A Hundred Stretches Hence / I Wish There Was No Prisons” joins two songs about prisons, from 1859 and 1961, while “Jowl, Jowl and Listen Lads” combines verses from mining songs to sharpen its account of unsafe work. The review notes that these themes remain pertinent amid debate over prison releases and scrutiny of workplace injury.

The review also singles out “Bold Captain Avery”, a song dating to 1694 that it says has not previously been recorded. Its story of a pirate who became a fantasy figure for oppressed workers offers a different kind of historical link: the collective’s performance brings a neglected song into the present-day recorded folk canon.

content.headline: China’s first fully AI-generated film flops, but investors still see a future
content.shortHeadline: China’s AI film flops as investors back the technology
content.standfirst: Sanxingdui: Future Past earned little at the box office, with one critic blaming its failure on an unentertaining film. Yet Chinese investors continue to pursue AI productions, drawn in part by the prospect of making films with much smaller crews.

image.caption: A scene from Sanxingdui: Future Past, China’s fully AI-generated feature film.

sources.originalTitle: China’s first AI-generated film is a flop. Some still see it as the future of cinema

segments.body: Sanxingdui: Future Past, described as China’s first fully AI-generated film, earned 1.7m yuan (£191,000) at the box office. Its producer said it cost “tens of millions” to make. The Guardian watched it in a nearly empty Beijing cinema and found it no worse than some human-made action films, despite confusing storytelling and awkward dialogue.

segments.title: Why the experiment matters
segments.body: The film’s visuals and some sound effects were made with AI; humans edited it. One screenwriter in Beijing said most of the projects she had recently been approached about were AI films, adding that investors believe the technology can reduce a production from 100 people to five. Independent critic Yu Yaqin offered a simpler explanation for this film’s poor performance: “the movie isn’t entertaining”.

The article sets the cinema flop against a growing Chinese market for AI-generated microdramas, which are uploaded to streaming platforms in large numbers and are estimated to be worth $3bn. It also raises a practical question: audiences may be reluctant to pay for a cinema ticket when similar content is free on a phone. The film’s failure has not settled whether AI will reshape production.

content.headline: Mum, I’m Alien Pregnant review: New Zealand comedy finds laughs in slime
content.shortHeadline: Mum, I’m Alien Pregnant finds comedy in the gross-out
content.standfirst: Hannah Lynch plays a woman facing an unexpected alien pregnancy in a deliberately silly comedy horror. The Guardian finds its deadpan cast and willingness to embrace the absurd more successful than any deeper allegory.

image.caption: Mary, played by Hannah Lynch, with her mother in Mum, I’m Alien Pregnant.

sources.originalTitle: Mum, I’m Alien Pregnant review – slime and silliness in amusing New Zealand comedy horror

segments.body: In this New Zealand comedy horror, thirtysomething underachiever Mary (Hannah Lynch) becomes pregnant after her shy neighbour Boo (Arlo Green) ejaculates on her with his tentacle-bearing alien penis. The film does not explain the anatomy, and the review suggests there is little point looking for a reason: its humour comes from how calmly the characters face increasingly bizarre events.

Supporting actors Yvette Parsons and Jackie van Beek play the mothers, who worry about the mess and domestic disruption as alien gristle and mucus arrive. The review says the cast understands the film’s underplayed tone. A reading of the story as a parable about single motherhood and pregnancy is possible, it adds, but slow comic turns and slime are the real attraction.

content.headline: Carrie at 50: Brian De Palma’s horror still cuts deep
content.shortHeadline: Carrie at 50: De Palma’s horror remains powerful
content.standfirst: Fifty years after its release, Sissy Spacek’s Carrie remains a landmark in film horror, argues the Guardian. Its split-screen style and silences make the prom-night humiliation feel both frightening and heartbreaking.

image.caption: Sissy Spacek as Carrie White in Brian De Palma’s 1976 film.

sources.originalTitle: Carrie at 50: Brian De Palma’s fiery masterpiece still has the power

segments.body: Brian De Palma’s 1976 adaptation of Stephen King’s Carrie turns 50 on 3 November. The film follows Carrie White, a bullied teenager with telekinetic powers, through the humiliation at her high-school prom and its bloody consequences. Sissy Spacek’s performance, especially the image of Carrie drenched in blood, helped make the story’s central figure indelible.

segments.title: A world made strange
segments.body: The review contrasts De Palma’s film with Mike Flanagan’s newer television adaptation, describing the older version as more frightening and more economical with dialogue. De Palma’s split-diopter shots keep characters in focus across the frame while emphasising their emotional distance; the rotating camera at the prom turns a moment of apparent acceptance into something dizzying.

The film’s final stretch relies on images and sound rather than extended explanation, making Spacek’s performance all the more affecting, the review says. Its final shock has kept this version of Carrie alive in the public imagination as a nightmare reflection of adolescence. The anniversary offers a chance to revisit a film whose influence has outlasted its original moment.

content.headline: Wicker’s basket-made romance turns into a 4DX spectacle—and a debate
content.shortHeadline: Wicker in 4DX: a wild screening and a gender debate
content.standfirst: Olivia Colman’s medieval romance with a wicker husband has found an unlikely second life in motion-seat cinemas. One account relishes the crowd’s delighted response; another argues the film’s fantasy of a man made to please his wife is knowingly, and uncomfortably, sexist.

image.caption: Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård in Wicker.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Screams on the level of a Taylor Swift concert’: horny romp Wicker gets the 4DX treatment
Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it

segments.body: Wicker pairs Olivia Colman’s Fisherwoman with Alexander Skarsgård as a husband woven from willow. The Guardian recounts a sold-out 4DX screening where moving seats and water effects amplified the film’s bed-breaking sex scene, prompting laughter and screams from an audience ready to play along. The format, usually associated with action films, made the romance an unexpected spectacle.

segments.title: Fantasy, with a thorn in it
segments.body: The i Paper review takes a different route into the film’s appeal. It calls Wicker funny and horny, but also argues that the husband’s lack of agency makes the story a gendered fairy tale: he exists to serve his wife, even when that means risking harm. The reviewer remains fond of the film while questioning what its fantasy suggests about unequal relationships.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s reviewer argues that the Wicker Husband’s devotion is a deliberately troubling fantasy: the film’s comedy depends on a man being made to satisfy his wife, with little attention to his own desires.

content.headline: The best films to watch in November, from Elsinore to The Hunger Games
content.shortHeadline: November films: Elsinore, The Hunger Games and more
content.standfirst: A month of cinema releases ranges from Andrew Scott as actor Ian Charleson to a new Hunger Games prequel and a drama about disability rights activist Judith Heumann. The BBC Culture guide also includes international drama, animation and a behind-the-scenes story about Rocky.

sources.originalTitle: Elsinore to The Hunger Games: 12 of the best films to watch in November

segments.body: BBC Culture’s November film guide leads with Elsinore, in which Andrew Scott plays actor Ian Charleson as he takes on Hamlet in the final months of his life. Olivia Colman and Billie Piper co-star. The guide describes the film as both heart-rending and joyous, and notes its release dates vary by territory, with the UK release scheduled for January.

segments.title: A broad month at the cinema
segments.body: The selection also includes Sunrise on the Reaping, a Hunger Games prequel, and Club Kid, Jordan Firstman’s comedy-drama about a New York party promoter who meets the son he did not know he had. Being Heumann dramatises disability-rights activist Judith Heumann’s 1977 protest in San Francisco, with Ruth Madeley in the lead role.

Other picks include I Play Rocky, about Sylvester Stallone writing the role that made him a star; Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine; and Ryūsuke Hamaguchi’s All of a Sudden. The guide is a forward-looking release calendar rather than a critical ranking, and its dates differ by country, so readers should check local availability.

content.headline: The French voices of Homer and Marge fell in love in the studio
content.shortHeadline: The Simpsons’ French Homer and Marge are a real couple
content.standfirst: Philippe Peythieu and Véronique Augereau have voiced Homer and Marge in the French dub of The Simpsons since 1990. They met through the show, married, and say recording together helped bring them closer.

image.caption: Homer and Marge Simpson in season 27 of The Simpsons.

sources.originalTitle: They fell in love on The Simpsons and married in real life. Meet the French Homer and Marge

segments.body: Philippe Peythieu and Véronique Augereau have voiced Homer and Marge in the French version of The Simpsons since 1990. The actors met while auditioning for the roles, initially as colleagues; recording the show brought them closer, and they eventually married. They still record together in a Paris studio for 10 to 12 days each year.

segments.title: A long-running partnership
segments.body: The pair say the show’s humour and spirit were part of what they loved from the beginning. Augereau describes Marge as tender toward Homer despite his foolishness, while Peythieu says the couple’s bond survives their differences. They have also met fans who tell them the French voices were part of their childhood.

Both actors reject the idea of artificial intelligence taking over their roles, with Augereau joking that they support “artistic intelligence”. Their story offers a human counterpoint to the show’s many years of international dubbing: for them, an enduring voice partnership became a lasting relationship off screen.

content.headline: The John Lewis Christmas advert turns shopping into an AI fable
content.shortHeadline: John Lewis’s Christmas ad imagines an AI-run future
content.standfirst: Kristin Scott Thomas stars as a grandmother whose wooden dog helps her find a gift, in a festive advert the Guardian reads as a satire of outsourcing human judgement to chatbots. Its seasonal retail setting does not soften the review’s dystopian joke.

image.caption: Kristin Scott Thomas in the 2026 John Lewis Christmas advert.

sources.originalTitle: The 2026 John Lewis Christmas advert is here – and it’s Kristin Scott Thomas v Pickles the evil AI overlord puppy!

segments.body: Kristin Scott Thomas plays a grandmother in the 2026 John Lewis Christmas advert. When her grandchildren pass her by, she reaches for a wooden dog named Pickles, which comes to life and takes her on a tour of shops before she returns with a present for them. The advert makes shopping its subject, but the Guardian’s review finds a darker thread in Pickles’ advice.

segments.title: A chatbot in a dog costume
segments.body: The review reads Pickles as an AI assistant: the grandmother relies on it to decide what to buy, and the advert’s ending, in which she prepares a room as a gift, is treated as a warning about outsourcing thought and choice. The piece turns that reading into an intentionally exaggerated joke about surveillance and a post-human Christmas.

content.headline: The Gilded Age returns to a barrage of period-drama clichés
content.shortHeadline: The Gilded Age review: a costume drama in a rut
content.standfirst: Julian Fellowes’ high-society series is back for a fourth season, but the Guardian’s critic finds its familiar plots and blunt dialogue more exhausting than entertaining. The review’s sharp verdict stands apart from a BBC guide that previews the season’s storylines.

image.caption: Christine Baranski and Cynthia Nixon in The Gilded Age.

sources.originalTitle: The Gilded Age review – what did we do to deserve such a terrible stinker?

segments.body: The Gilded Age begins its fourth season with Gladys in a difficult childbirth and Oscar preparing to marry Enid, a widow with money. In New York, Agnes is looking forward to hosting the president, while Marian remains drawn to Larry and Peggy faces tensions with her future mother-in-law. The Guardian review sees these plotlines as a rapid assembly of period-drama clichés.

segments.title: A critic’s verdict
segments.body: The review mocks the show’s exposition-heavy dialogue and familiar turns, from a medical emergency to romantic complications after a coach accident. It also points to the series’ treatment of race and class as unsubtle. Its judgement is unequivocal: the new season feels much like the old one, with the critic calling it “uniformly terrible”.

content.headline: The One About Matthew Perry review: a painful, intrusive retelling
content.shortHeadline: Matthew Perry’s documentary tells little the memoir didn’t
content.standfirst: Netflix’s three-part series revisits the Friends actor’s addiction and death, but the i Paper argues that his own memoir told the story more powerfully. It questions what the documentary adds by asking loved ones to revisit painful moments.

sources.originalTitle: Netflix’s Matthew Perry documentary is undignified and intrusive

segments.body: The One About Matthew Perry revisits the actor’s life, addiction and death at 54 in 2023. The i Paper review notes that Perry had already written in detail about his struggles in his 2022 memoir, Friends, Lovers and the Big Terrible Thing. With family, friends and archive footage, the documentary is often moving, but the review says much of its account feels second-hand.

segments.title: What does the access add?
segments.body: The review is most critical of the series’ treatment of Perry’s death and the people around him. It says the documentary moves quickly through unanswered questions about the ketamine supply and the exploitation of wealthy addicts, while dwelling on relatives’ grief. The reviewer asks whether the interviews serve Perry’s memory or primarily provide the access the production needs.

The reviewer acknowledges the tenderness in stories of Perry’s generosity and in the surviving Friends cast attending his funeral together. But the overall verdict is that the series brings little new understanding and risks retraumatising people who loved him. The piece argues that Perry’s own words and performances remain the more respectful record of his life.

content.headline: A veteran games presenter becomes the hero of an indie horror game
content.shortHeadline: From GamesMaster to indie horror-game hero
content.standfirst: After 50 years of playing games, the Guardian writer is voicing the protagonist of Black Tides: Draga’s Wake. He describes the strange work of inventing fight sounds in a rural garage and the moment his children recognised his voice.

image.caption: Draga, the protagonist of Black Tides: Draga’s Wake.

sources.originalTitle: After 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in one

segments.body: The Guardian’s writer was asked to voice Draga, a tough sailor infected by an ancient god, in Black Tides: Draga’s Wake, a survival horror game set aboard a decaying steamship. After early attempts felt wrong, he lowered his voice and stopped trying to act so hard, a change he says worked with the character.

segments.title: Making a game together
segments.body: The game is being developed by a distributed team working in spare time, a process the writer compares with the bedroom programming culture of the ZX Spectrum era. One of the strangest tasks was recording improvised fight noises for the developers to place in the game. He says the work has made him newly attentive to the craft of voice acting and directing in games.

The most affecting moment came when he played clips for his children without telling them he was in the game. Their delight when they recognised their father as a horror-game hero became one of his favourite memories as a parent. The game’s announcement trailer had drawn 200,000 views in its first few days, and its creator was in discussions with publishers.

content.headline: Night Plane review: a flight attendant’s shift becomes a horror trip
content.shortHeadline: Night Plane turns airport routine into indie horror
content.standfirst: This retro-style horror game begins with check-ins and trolley service before sending its flight attendant through a looping nightmare of demons, flickering lights and strange passengers. The Guardian praises its eerie detail and comic timing.

image.caption: A scene from the retro-style horror game Night Plane.

sources.originalTitle: Night Plane review – join the jumbo jet to hell in this indie horror head trip

segments.body: Night Plane casts the player as a flight attendant. At first, the work is routine: checking tickets, serving passengers and handling complaints. Then the plane crashes, and the player finds themself back at the airport, where some customers may be demons in disguise. The game’s central uncertainty is whether the player is dead, in purgatory or somewhere stranger.

segments.title: A joke with a sting
segments.body: Liquid Static Studio uses low-poly visuals inspired by the original PlayStation era to make passengers and airport spaces unsettling. The review describes a mix of flickering cabin lights, strange noises and disjointed dialogue, alongside dry jokes that can arrive just before a jump scare. The game’s initial air of horror spoof gives way to genuinely disturbing images.

The Guardian finds the game clever and absorbing, with new quests and endings to uncover on repeat playthroughs. It estimates a first run at four or five hours and calls the price, under £10, a bargain. The review also places Night Plane among horror games that use familiar game conventions—here, repetitive work—to explore existential unease.

content.headline: The White House’s new arcade uses familiar games to target migrants
content.shortHeadline: White House arcade turns games into anti-migrant propaganda
content.standfirst: A collection of pixel-art mini-games repurposes familiar formats to promote the Trump administration’s political messaging, including games that dehumanise migrants. The Guardian argues that the arcade shows how easily play can be weaponised.

image.caption: A screenshot from Build the Wall, one of the White House Arcade games.

sources.originalTitle: The Trump White House’s fetish for gamer culture has moved up a level with new arcade

segments.body: The White House has released a web arcade of games styled after familiar titles. Among them, Build the Wall turns Tetris into a border-fortification challenge, while Rio Run has the player collect brown figures in orange jumpsuits. The Guardian describes the games as propaganda wrapped in a nostalgic pixel-art look.

segments.title: A political use for play
segments.body: The article argues that the arcade extends earlier efforts to use game imagery in political messaging. It cites author George Osborn, who says gaming culture has been part of the political right’s communications strategy and that putting games directly on the White House website marks an escalation from posting game-coded content on social media.

The writer calls the games mean-spirited and unimaginative, but cautions that outrage can still help draw people into the intended culture-war argument. The larger concern, the article says, is that games’ ability to persuade and shape culture should not be overlooked, particularly as political and financial interests gain influence in the industry.

content.headline: Scientists report possible red blood cell traces in a 115m-year-old dinosaur
content.shortHeadline: Possible blood cell traces found in a 115m-year-old dinosaur fossil
content.standfirst: Researchers say structures in a Brazilian dinosaur bone resemble red blood cells, and tests detected heme. The interpretation is disputed, but could offer new ways to study what fossils preserve.

image.caption: Prof Kliti Grice with fossilised remains of the Aratasaurus, which lived in Brazil 115m years ago.

sources.originalTitle: Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientists

segments.body: Researchers examining the hind-leg bone of an Aratasaurus, a meat-eating dinosaur from what is now north-eastern Brazil, found small structures resembling red blood cells in channels where blood vessels once ran. Chemical tests detected heme, a component of haemoglobin, along with traces of collagen’s amino-acid building blocks.

segments.title: A striking claim, still under debate
segments.body: The researchers suggest that the mineral hausmannite may have helped preserve the structures and molecules. But palaeontologist Mary Schweitzer questions whether the concave shapes are red blood cells: she says dinosaur cells should have a dome-like bulge. She is more persuaded by the heme and collagen findings. The study does not claim that DNA or large proteins survive in the fossil.

content.headline: Pompeii wardrobe yields jewellery, coins and a child’s charm necklace
content.shortHeadline: A sealed Pompeii wardrobe reveals a child’s charm necklace
content.standfirst: Objects left behind in a home buried by Vesuvius include a perfume bottle, coins and a necklace traditionally worn by children. The finds offer a glimpse of domestic life in the Roman city before the eruption.

image.caption: Personal belongings found in a Pompeii home on Via dell’Abbondanza.

sources.originalTitle: Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe

segments.body: Archaeologists found personal objects in a wooden wardrobe in a Pompeii home on Via dell’Abbondanza, sealed since the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79. The finds include tweezers, a small glass perfume bottle, an incense burner, a bronze lantern and 38 bronze coins.

segments.title: A necklace with a purpose
segments.body: The most distinctive object is a necklace with more than 20 charms, including figures of the gods Bes and Mercury. Known as a crepundia, this type of necklace was traditionally worn by children; its charms rattled, helping parents keep track of them and potentially identify them. The coins and household goods may suggest the occupants fled in a hurry, but that remains an interpretation.

content.headline: NASA’s Swift space telescope is expected to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere
content.shortHeadline: NASA’s Swift telescope is expected to fall back to Earth
content.standfirst: The ageing observatory is forecast to re-enter on Wednesday, with NASA expecting most of it to burn up. The agency estimates the chance of surviving debris harming anyone is low, but continues to monitor its descent.

sources.originalTitle: A truck-sized NASA space telescope is about to crash to Earth

segments.body: NASA expects its Swift Observatory to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday, with the forecast time uncertain by as much as 11 hours. The agency says most of the spacecraft should burn up, although some parts may survive. Its estimate of the risk of harm to anyone on Earth is about one in 2,100.

segments.title: A long-running mission ends
segments.body: The observatory, launched almost 22 years ago to study gamma-ray bursts, went on to serve as a general-purpose multiwavelength telescope. NASA abandoned an attempt to raise its orbit after the spacecraft intended to help encountered technical problems. The agency says the possible debris landing zone is limited to latitudes between 20.6 degrees north and south, and it will continue to update its predictions.

content.headline: Venus, the Moon and Spica will meet in the dawn sky on 7 November
content.shortHeadline: Look for Venus, the Moon and Spica before dawn on 7 November
content.standfirst: The three objects will appear low in the east-south-east before sunrise. A clear horizon is needed to see the grouping, and the Moon will be a slim crescent with a chance of seeing its faint earthshine.

image.caption: Illustration of Venus, Spica and the Moon in the sky before dawn on 7 November.

sources.originalTitle: Starwatch: Catch the striking trifecta of Venus, the moon and Spica at break of dawn

segments.body: Early risers on 7 November can look east-south-east before dawn for bright Venus beside Spica, the brightest star in Virgo, and a thin waning crescent Moon. From London, the view is forecast for 0600 GMT; the three objects will be low above the horizon, so a clear view in that direction will help.

The Moon will be two days from new, with about 4% of its Earth-facing side illuminated. In dark conditions, its unlit portion may also be faintly visible, lit by sunlight reflected from Earth—a phenomenon known as earthshine. The grouping will also be visible from the southern hemisphere, where it will appear higher in the eastern sky.

content.headline: Binance says hackers used fake job interviews and a compromised AI tool
content.shortHeadline: Binance says fake interviews helped hackers breach its systems
content.standfirst: The exchange says attackers used a bogus recruitment process to compromise an engineer’s computer, then accessed other devices and an internal AI tool. US agencies blame North Korea, which denies involvement.

image.caption: Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange targeted in the $6.3bn hack.

sources.originalTitle: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after largest-ever crypto hack

segments.body: Binance says an engineer was approached on a legitimate job-hunting platform and persuaded to download malware disguised as an interview assignment. The company says attackers then used the compromised laptop and an internal AI tool to reach two other engineers’ computers and carry out further steps in the $6.3bn theft.

segments.title: Attribution remains contested
segments.body: The FBI and other US agencies have attributed the hack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, an accusation Pyongyang denies. Binance says it is working with law enforcement and has replenished 98% of affected token assets. The exchange has not completed its investigation, and North Korea’s denial does not resolve who was responsible.

perspectives.body: North Korea calls the allegations a political provocation and says it opposes malicious activity in cyberspace. The BBC reports that the country has consistently denied similar accusations.

segments.body: The breach forced Binance to suspend withdrawals globally. The exchange says it has set aside more than the funds needed to cover the loss; it also reports that users withdrew billions after service resumed. Those are the company’s figures, and the full investigation is not complete.

content.headline: Cyberattacks on European freezers also hit UK food suppliers
content.shortHeadline: Freezer cyberattacks reach UK food suppliers
content.standfirst: UK meat suppliers report refrigeration units being tampered with after attacks on shops across Europe. No stock was lost at the affected UK businesses, but officials and researchers warn that exposed, outdated systems remain a concern.

image.caption: A supermarket refrigeration unit in Sweden, where some units were affected by a cyber incident.

sources.originalTitle: UK meat industry hit by cyber-attack which targeted European supermarket freezers
Freezers of UK meat suppliers heat up after cyber-attacks in Europe
If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?

segments.body: The National Cyber Security Centre says it is aware of a small number of cases in which vulnerable technology was exploited in the UK. The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers says two members found fridges defrosting and another saw a unit reach 100C; the affected equipment was empty, so no produce was lost. No UK grocery chain has been directly affected.

segments.title: Who is responsible for securing the equipment?
segments.body: The attacks have affected retailers in several European countries, following similar incidents in France. The UK cyber agency says it is too early to identify those behind the latest incidents. Researchers found 256 attempted attacks on decoy refrigeration controls, with some infrastructure overlapping with systems previously associated with Russian-linked operations; they cannot identify a responsible group.

Researchers have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with UK retailers that are accessible over the public internet. That does not mean they can be hacked, but weak passwords or software flaws could expose them. Cybersecurity experts say retailers need to be clear about who is responsible for keeping connected equipment secure, not just who repairs it.

content.headline: Apple’s foldable iPhone sells out as memory costs and supply constraints rise
content.shortHeadline: Apple’s foldable iPhone sells out amid supply constraints
content.standfirst: Apple says it cannot yet predict when supply of its new foldable phone will catch up with demand. The company also reports rising memory costs as AI data centres compete for components.

image.caption: A customer holds the foldable iPhone Duo at Apple’s Fifth Avenue store in New York.

sources.originalTitle: Apple unsure when it will get more foldable iPhones ahead of Christmas
Apple warns of ‘unprecedented’ rise in memory chip prices

segments.body: Apple says its new iPhone Duo sold out just over a week after launch, and it cannot say when more will be available. Executives cite constraints in sourcing components and describe it as difficult to predict when supply and demand will balance. The roughly $2,000 phone is the company’s first major iPhone design change in nearly two decades.

segments.title: Costs are rising across the industry
segments.body: Apple chief executive John Ternus also described memory-price increases as unprecedented. The Guardian reports that Apple said higher memory costs will weigh on margins, even after price rises on iPads, MacBooks and iPhones offset some of the impact. Demand from AI data centres has driven up memory prices, adding to pressure on device makers.

content.headline: New York mayor criticises Madison Square Garden owner’s surveillance technology
content.shortHeadline: New York mayor challenges MSG owner over surveillance
content.standfirst: Zohran Mamdani says facial recognition and other surveillance technologies should not be allowed in public places. The dispute follows reporting about Madison Square Garden’s tracking systems and a proposed city ban on biometric-data collection.

sources.originalTitle: New York City’s Mamdani criticizes Madison Square Garden owner over surveillance tech

segments.body: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has criticised Madison Square Garden’s owner, saying its surveillance technology reflects problems with how such systems are used. He backed draft city legislation introduced by council member Shahana Hanif that would ban collecting biometric data, including through facial recognition, in public places.

segments.title: A dispute over what the company records
segments.body: The comments follow Wired reporting that the company uses cameras and face-scanning technology to track people in and around its venues, and keeps a database that reportedly labels some visitors, including performers, as “LGBTQIA” for unclear reasons. MSG called Wired’s reporting inaccurate and false and said it was pursuing legal remedies, but provided no evidence for that claim to TechCrunch.

content.headline: Bambu Lab’s nine-nozzle 3D printer pushes home printing towards multi-materials
content.shortHeadline: A nine-nozzle printer points to 3D printing’s next step
content.standfirst: The $2,499 H3C can switch among nine printheads and combine colours, materials and nozzle sizes. Early reviews show impressive possibilities, but also print failures and design quirks in a machine aimed at experienced users.

sources.originalTitle: Bambu’s nine-nozzle H3C foretells the future of 3D printing
Bambu Lab’s Newest Flagship Is a Behemoth in More Ways Than One

segments.body: Bambu Lab’s H3C stores nine printheads and can switch between them in about six seconds, allowing a print to combine colours, rigid and flexible materials, and different nozzle sizes. The Verge reviewer used it to make a coloured feather and a watch housing with an integrated flexible band. The printer costs $2,499.

segments.title: Promising, but not a finished verdict
segments.body: CNET’s testing also found the printer can produce complex models, including with different filament diameters, but reported failed tall prints when supports or purge towers fell. The Verge reviewer noted setup and software problems and warned that some flexible filament could jam in one slot. Both accounts describe early testing, not a complete assessment of long-term reliability.

content.headline: CPS prosecutor cited a fictional legal case after an AI search result
content.shortHeadline: CPS prosecutor cited a fictitious case after AI-assisted search
content.standfirst: A senior prosecutor relied on a nonexistent precedent in a case involving a child, court documents show. Judges said the explanation was unsatisfactory; the CPS says an internet search produced an AI summary and that it reviewed the error.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A serious failure’: CPS prosecutor cites imaginary case to high court after AI search

segments.body: A senior Crown Prosecution Service prosecutor cited a case that did not exist while arguing that an 11-year-old should face prosecution. The Guardian understands the reference came from an AI-generated summary during an internet search. The High Court said the false citation did not change the outcome of the child’s challenge; the case is due to go to trial in youth court.

segments.title: Checks and accountability
segments.body: Two senior High Court judges called the prosecutor’s explanation unsatisfactory. The CPS said the error came from internet legal research, that it had been remedied and that an internal review found no other affected cases. It says its policy requires human checks and bars AI from making legal decisions. A barrister’s tracker lists 101 confirmed, suspected or disputed AI-related errors and false citations, which its compiler says may be only a fraction of the total.

content.headline: UK AI data-centre plans raise questions over farmland, gas and emissions
content.shortHeadline: AI data-centre plans test UK climate and land-use commitments
content.standfirst: A Norfolk proposal could cover nearly 4,700 acres, while separate projects are considering gas generation as they wait for grid connections. The plans sharpen questions about how the AI buildout will affect farmland, local communities and emissions.

image.caption: Drax power station in North Yorkshire, where a data-centre development is planned.

sources.originalTitle: AI data centres could undermine UK's emissions goals
Huge data centre plan sees hundreds attend meeting
UK’s most polluting power plant could power country’s largest AI datacentre

segments.body: The BBC reports that four planned hyperscale data centres are considering gas-fired power while waiting for grid connections. If run continuously at full capacity, the projects could require 1.3 gigawatts and produce an estimated 4.1 million tonnes of carbon emissions a year, according to the BBC’s calculations. The government says on-site generation will be tightly controlled and time-limited.

segments.title: Local land and energy trade-offs
segments.body: One separate proposal, in Norfolk, would combine a large data centre and solar farms across 4,695 acres of farmland. At a public meeting, residents and a local farmer raised concerns about losing high-quality agricultural land, as well as noise and landscape impacts. In another proposal, Drax has agreed to develop a data centre with an eventual capacity above one gigawatt at its North Yorkshire site; its first phase is expected to use grid access, with direct supply from the power plant a later ambition.

perspectives.body: Farmer James Kitchen says the Norfolk site’s soil is productive, while campaigners and local residents argue that the project should be smaller or built on brownfield land. The developer says it welcomes consultation and will consider site-specific mitigation.

content.headline: Google will let schools switch off AI tools—but not keep Search
content.shortHeadline: Schools may have to accept Google AI to keep Search
content.standfirst: Google says schools can disable its AI tools for pupils next year, but schools that turn AI off altogether will also lose access to Google Search. The choice raises questions for schools that want conventional web search without AI features.

sources.originalTitle: Google will let schools disable its AI tools, but not without sacrificing Search

segments.body: Google plans to switch off AI tools for K–12 students next year unless school administrators choose to enable them. But the company says schools that restrict AI altogether will also lose Google Search, because AI features are now integrated into the search engine. That could leave schools choosing between AI features they may not want and a search tool they still rely on.

The change affects Gemini, NotebookLM, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search. Google says it will provide more details in the coming months and aims to give school leaders control over how its products are used. It is also introducing Guided Learning, an AI tutor-style tool intended to build understanding rather than simply provide answers.

content.headline: Google’s Dreambeans brings AI-generated personal stories to India, with privacy
content.shortHeadline: Google takes its personal AI stories app to India
content.standfirst: Dreambeans draws on connected Google services to create illustrated stories without a prompt. Its India launch adds 13 languages, while download figures and the app’s access to personal account data raise questions about its appeal and privacy.

sources.originalTitle: Google takes Dreambeans to India in bid to bring AI-generated personal stories to the masses

segments.body: Google has launched its experimental Dreambeans app in India, adding support for 13 languages. It uses information from services including Calendar, Gmail, Photos, Search and YouTube to generate illustrated stories about a user’s interests and daily life, without a prompt. Google says it chose India because of strong interest and widespread use of its services there.

segments.title: Personalisation and control
segments.body: Sensor Tower estimates Dreambeans has had nearly 55,000 US downloads since June, with downloads falling to about 5,500 in October. The app’s reliance on personal account information raises privacy questions. Google says users can choose which services to connect, disconnect them and delete Dreambeans data. The company also acknowledges that stories could surface upsetting subjects, such as people who have died.

Although the app supports several widely spoken Indian languages, it can generate stories in only one language at a time, not a mix such as Hindi and English. Google says it is exploring ways for Dreambeans to help users act on its suggestions, beyond generating stories.

content.headline: Apple raises App Store age ratings for dating and romantic AI apps
content.shortHeadline: Apple will rate dating and romantic AI apps 18-plus
content.standfirst: New App Store rules require an adult rating for apps with dating or relationship features, including virtual companions. Developers must also disclose location-sharing features, which can affect ratings in some regions.

sources.originalTitle: Apple is restricting dating apps and romanceable chatbots to over 18s
Apple restricts dating apps and AI companions to users 18 and up

segments.body: Apple will require apps with dating and relationship features to carry an 18-plus App Store rating. Developers must declare whether an app enables dating, relationship or sexual behaviour between real people or virtual companions. The updated questionnaire begins on 16 November, and developers must complete the new declarations by 12 January 2027.

segments.title: Virtual companions and location sharing
segments.body: The rules also cover AI companion apps that allow romantic or sexual interactions, including apps where that is one feature among many. Developers must disclose when an app shares a user’s real-world location with others; the effect on its minimum age rating will vary by region. TechCrunch reports that major AI companion apps have been downloaded 220 million times globally, according to figures it cites.

content.headline: Y Combinator’s Garry Tan says AI agents cost him up to $200,000 a year
content.shortHeadline: Garry Tan says he spends up to $200,000 a year on AI agents
content.standfirst: The startup accelerator chief says his agents work across projects and personal files, including email and therapy notes. His account illustrates both the reach and the cost of intensive agent use—and the sensitivity of the information involved.

sources.originalTitle: Y Combinator’s Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens

segments.body: Garry Tan, chief executive of Y Combinator, says he spends about $100,000 to $200,000 a year on AI tokens. He uses agents for work and coding, and says one has read his email, Dropbox, Apple Notes and therapy notes spanning 20 years. He describes the tools as helping with both tasks and day-to-day decisions.

segments.title: A cost and control problem
segments.body: Tan says the expense is a privilege that most people cannot afford and argues that costs need to fall for personal agents to become mainstream. He also says he would like a personal AI that users control, rather than one controlled by a large technology company. The account is an individual example, not evidence of how representative this level of use is.

content.headline: Everton deepen Newcastle crisis as Barry keeps scoring and Grealish remains out
content.shortHeadline: Everton deepen Newcastle crisis; Barry scores again
content.standfirst: Everton’s 1-0 win at St James’ Park lifted them to seventh and left Newcastle with a fourth defeat in six league games. Thierno Barry scored again, while Jack Grealish’s return remains unclear.

sources.originalTitle: Jeers again as home woes continue - Jaissle has big problems at Newcastle
From nightmare debut season to Everton hero - Barry's revival
Grealish can still have Everton future - Moyes
